title: GCSE Pseudocode Tutor
tagline: Static reference for a home tutor. One idea a day. Print one snippet at a time.

print.studentHint: Predict first. Then trace every state change.
print.footer: Code changes state. Trace the state.

copy.selectHint: Pick a day. Print the snippet. Keep the key on this screen.

phases.title: Arrays and strings
phases.blurb: Index, scan, accumulate, search, two pointers.

phases.title: Algorithms
phases.blurb: Search, nested loops, sort, and work-size intuition.

phases.title: Data structures
phases.blurb: Stack, queue, linked list, and maps.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.idea: A variable holds one value. Assignment replaces that value.
lessons.cue: Cover the names. Ask for a and b at the end before any tracing.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
a <- 4
b <- 9
temp <- a
a <- b
b <- temp
OUTPUT a
OUTPUT b
predict: What is a at the end?
What is b at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It copies a aside, then moves b into a, then moves the saved copy into b.
lessons.name: assignment / swap
lessons.change: Swap x and y instead of a and b. Same three lines.
lessons.stretch: Rotate three values: a into b, b into c, c into a.
lessons.key: a is 9. b is 4. temp ends as 4.

lessons.title: Arithmetic
lessons.idea: Expressions compute a new value. Store it if you need it later.
lessons.cue: Ask for total first, then average. Watch integer vs real if it comes up.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
total <- 12 + 8 + 10
count <- 3
average <- total / count
OUTPUT total
OUTPUT average
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It adds three scores, then divides by how many scores there were.
lessons.name: total / average
lessons.change: Add a fourth score of 6. What changes?
lessons.stretch: Compute the average of 5, 5, and 8 without a total variable. Why is total useful?
lessons.key: total is 30. average is 10.

lessons.title: Boolean expressions
lessons.idea: A Boolean is TRUE or FALSE. Comparisons produce Booleans.
lessons.cue: Ask them to say TRUE or FALSE, not yes or no.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
n <- 14
even <- (n MOD 2) = 0
OUTPUT even
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It tests whether dividing n by 2 leaves no remainder.
lessons.name: Boolean / even test / MOD
lessons.change: Change it so even is TRUE for odd numbers.
lessons.stretch: What is even when n is 0?
lessons.key: n MOD 2 is 0. even is TRUE.

lessons.title: IF / ELSE
lessons.idea: A condition chooses one path. The other path is skipped.
lessons.cue: Ask which branch runs before they read the assignments.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
a <- 7
b <- 11
IF a > b THEN
    larger <- a
ELSE
    larger <- b
ENDIF
OUTPUT larger
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It keeps the number that is bigger.
lessons.name: selection / max of two
lessons.change: Find the smaller number instead.
lessons.stretch: What happens if a and b are equal? Change the code to report a tie.
lessons.key: a > b is FALSE. larger is 11.

lessons.title: Nested conditions
lessons.idea: An IF inside an ELSE checks the next band only if earlier bands failed.
lessons.cue: Walk the tests from the top. Stop at the first true one.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
score <- 73
IF score >= 80 THEN
    grade <- "A"
ELSE
    IF score >= 70 THEN
        grade <- "B"
    ELSE
        IF score >= 60 THEN
            grade <- "C"
        ELSE
            grade <- "U"
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
ENDIF
OUTPUT grade
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It maps a score onto the first matching grade band.
lessons.name: nested selection / grade boundaries
lessons.change: Add a grade A* for 90 and above.
lessons.stretch: What grade does 70 get? What grade does 69 get?
lessons.key: 73 is not >= 80. It is >= 70. grade is B.

lessons.title: FOR loop
lessons.idea: A FOR loop repeats a body. The loop variable steps through a range.
lessons.cue: Build the table row by row. Do not jump to the formula for 1 to n.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
n <- 5
sum <- 0
FOR i <- 1 TO n
    sum <- sum + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT sum
predict: How many times does the body run?
What is sum at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It adds each whole number from 1 to n into a running total.
lessons.name: FOR loop / accumulator
lessons.change: Sum only the even values from 1 to n.
lessons.stretch: What is sum when n is 1? When n is 0, this loop body does not run.
lessons.key: Body runs 5 times. sum is 15.

lessons.title: WHILE loop
lessons.idea: WHILE repeats while a condition stays true. The body must change that condition.
lessons.cue: Watch n on every row. Ask when the condition becomes false.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
n <- 5
WHILE n > 0
    OUTPUT n
    n <- n - 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT "done"
predict: What is n after the loop?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It prints a countdown, then stops when n is no longer greater than 0.
lessons.name: WHILE / countdown
lessons.change: Count up from 1 until n, using WHILE.
lessons.stretch: What happens if you forget n <- n - 1?
lessons.key: Prints 5 4 3 2 1 then done. n ends as 0.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.idea: A function is a named block. A call jumps in, then returns.
lessons.cue: Trace into square(6). Then come back to OUTPUT.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
FUNCTION square(x)
    RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT square(6)
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It takes one number and returns that number times itself.
lessons.name: function call / parameter / return
lessons.change: Add a function cube(x) and output cube(3).
lessons.stretch: What does square(square(2)) print?
lessons.key: x is 6. printed value is 36.

lessons.title: Return values
lessons.idea: A function can choose a value with IF, then hand that value back.
lessons.cue: Ask which RETURN runs. Only one RETURN runs.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
FUNCTION maxOf(a, b)
    IF a > b THEN
        RETURN a
    ELSE
        RETURN b
    ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT maxOf(9, 4)
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It compares two values and returns the larger one.
lessons.name: return value / function selection
lessons.change: Write minOf(a, b) using the same shape.
lessons.stretch: What does maxOf(5, 5) return?
lessons.key: a > b is TRUE. printed value is 9.

lessons.title: Array indexing
lessons.idea: An array holds many values. An index picks one slot.
lessons.cue: Say the indexes out loud: 0, 1, 2, 3. Then change index 2.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [4, 8, 15, 16]
OUTPUT nums[0]
nums[2] <- 99
OUTPUT nums[2]
OUTPUT nums
predict: What does nums contain at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It reads the first slot, then overwrites the slot at index 2.
lessons.name: index / element / update
lessons.change: Set the last element to 0. Which index is that?
lessons.stretch: What happens if you use nums[4] on this array?
lessons.key: Prints 4, then 99, then [4, 8, 99, 16].

lessons.title: Array traversal
lessons.idea: A loop plus an index visits every element.
lessons.cue: Keep i and nums[i] in separate columns.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [5, 2, 9]
FOR i <- 0 TO 2
    OUTPUT nums[i]
NEXT i
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It walks from the first slot to the last slot and prints each value.
lessons.name: traversal / linear scan
lessons.change: Print the array from last to first.
lessons.stretch: Rewrite the loop as FOR i <- 0 TO LEN(nums) - 1.
lessons.key: Prints 5, 2, 9. i takes 0, 1, 2.

lessons.title: Accumulator pattern
lessons.idea: One variable collects a running result while you scan.
lessons.cue: Write sum before and after each add. Do not add in your head only.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [5, 2, 9, 4]
sum <- 0
FOR i <- 0 TO 3
    sum <- sum + nums[i]
NEXT i
OUTPUT sum
predict: What is sum after the first add?
What is sum at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It adds every element into one running total.
lessons.name: accumulator
lessons.change: Accumulate the product instead of the sum. Start product at 1.
lessons.stretch: What is the right start value if you sum an empty array?
lessons.key: sum goes 5, 7, 16, 20. Final sum is 20.

lessons.title: Minimum / maximum pattern
lessons.idea: Remember the best value seen so far. Replace it when you see a better one.
lessons.cue: Start best at nums[0]. Then walk the rest.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [5, 2, 9, 4]
best <- nums[0]
FOR i <- 1 TO 3
    IF nums[i] > best THEN
        best <- nums[i]
    ENDIF
NEXT i
OUTPUT best
predict: What is best after i is 1?
What is best at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It remembers the largest value seen so far.
lessons.name: maximum / best-so-far
lessons.change: Find the smallest value instead.
lessons.stretch: Why is starting best at 0 wrong for this array? It is not wrong here, but it fails for all-negative arrays.
lessons.key: After i=1, best is still 5. Final best is 9.

lessons.title: Counter pattern
lessons.idea: A counter goes up by one when a condition matches.
lessons.cue: Tick the counter only on a match. Leave it on a miss.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [7, 2, 7, 9, 7]
count <- 0
FOR i <- 0 TO 4
    IF nums[i] = 7 THEN
        count <- count + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT i
OUTPUT count
predict: How many times does count go up?
What is count at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It counts how many times 7 appears.
lessons.name: counter
lessons.change: Count the even numbers instead of the 7s.
lessons.stretch: What is count if the array has no 7?
lessons.key: count goes up 3 times. Final count is 3.

lessons.title: Linear search
lessons.idea: Scan from the start. Stop when you find the target, or when the array ends.
lessons.cue: Ask when found becomes TRUE. The loop then stops.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [4, 8, 15, 16, 23]
target <- 16
found <- FALSE
pos <- -1
i <- 0
WHILE i <= 4 AND found = FALSE
    IF nums[i] = target THEN
        found <- TRUE
        pos <- i
    ENDIF
    i <- i + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT found
OUTPUT pos
predict: What is pos? How many tests ran?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It looks at each element until it finds the target, then remembers that index.
lessons.name: linear search / flag
lessons.change: Search for 10 instead. What are found and pos?
lessons.stretch: Change it so it finds the last 16 if the array has two of them.
lessons.key: found is TRUE. pos is 3. It tests indexes 0 to 3.

lessons.title: Strings as sequences
lessons.idea: A string is a sequence of characters. You can index it like an array.
lessons.cue: Treat each letter as one element. Count only the matches.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
word <- "banana"
count <- 0
FOR i <- 0 TO LEN(word) - 1
    IF word[i] = "a" THEN
        count <- count + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT i
OUTPUT count
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It counts how many times the letter a appears.
lessons.name: string scan / counter
lessons.change: Count the letter n instead.
lessons.stretch: What is count for "aaa"? For ""?
lessons.key: LEN(word) is 6. count is 3.

lessons.title: Two pointers
lessons.idea: Two indexes can walk toward each other and swap as they meet.
lessons.cue: Fill left, right, and the whole array after every swap.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
items <- ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]
left <- 0
right <- 4
WHILE left < right
    temp <- items[left]
    items[left] <- items[right]
    items[right] <- temp
    left <- left + 1
    right <- right - 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT items
predict: What is items after the first swap?
What is items at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It swaps the ends, then moves inward, until the two indexes meet.
lessons.name: two pointers / reverse
lessons.change: Reverse only the first four letters, leaving E in place.
lessons.stretch: Does the middle letter C ever swap? Why not?
lessons.key: After swap 1: [E, B, C, D, A]. Final: [E, D, C, B, A]. C stays in the middle.

lessons.title: Palindrome
lessons.idea: A palindrome reads the same from both ends. Compare left and right.
lessons.cue: One mismatch is enough to fail. Do not keep comparing after a fail.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
word <- "level"
left <- 0
right <- LEN(word) - 1
ok <- TRUE
WHILE left < right AND ok = TRUE
    IF word[left] != word[right] THEN
        ok <- FALSE
    ENDIF
    left <- left + 1
    right <- right - 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT ok
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It checks that each pair of letters from the outside matches.
lessons.name: palindrome / two pointers / flag
lessons.change: Try the same code on "lemon". Where does it fail?
lessons.stretch: Is a one-letter word a palindrome with this code?
lessons.key: Pairs: l/l, e/e. ok is TRUE.

lessons.title: Linear search revisited
lessons.idea: Count comparisons. First match stops the search.
lessons.cue: Ask how many comparisons for first, middle, missing.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [11, 42, 7, 42, 19]
target <- 42
comparisons <- 0
pos <- -1
i <- 0
WHILE i <= 4 AND pos = -1
    comparisons <- comparisons + 1
    IF nums[i] = target THEN
        pos <- i
    ENDIF
    i <- i + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT pos
OUTPUT comparisons
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It finds the first 42 and counts how many tests that took.
lessons.name: linear search / comparisons
lessons.change: Search for 19. How many comparisons then?
lessons.stretch: Search for 5. What are pos and comparisons?
lessons.key: pos is 1. comparisons is 2. The second 42 is never tested.

lessons.title: Binary search
lessons.idea: On a sorted array, throw away half the remaining range each step.
lessons.cue: Keep low, high, mid, and the value at mid. Recalculate mid every row.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
array <- [3, 8, 12, 19, 24, 31, 40]
target <- 24
low <- 0
high <- 6
found <- FALSE
mid <- -1
WHILE low <= high AND found = FALSE
    mid <- (low + high) DIV 2
    IF array[mid] = target THEN
        found <- TRUE
    ELSE
        IF array[mid] < target THEN
            low <- mid + 1
        ELSE
            high <- mid - 1
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT found
OUTPUT mid
predict: What are found and mid at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It looks at the middle of the live range, then keeps the half that can still hold the target.
lessons.name: binary search / divide and conquer
lessons.change: Search for 3. Search for 40. Search for 10.
lessons.stretch: Why must the array be sorted?
lessons.key: mid takes 3, then 5, then 4. found is TRUE. mid ends as 4.

lessons.title: Nested loops
lessons.idea: An inner loop finishes all of its turns for each outer turn.
lessons.cue: Write a row for every (i, j) pair. Cross out i = j.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nums <- [2, 5, 9]
FOR i <- 0 TO 2
    FOR j <- 0 TO 2
        IF i != j THEN
            OUTPUT nums[i]
            OUTPUT nums[j]
        ENDIF
    NEXT j
NEXT i
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It compares every value with every different value.
lessons.name: nested iteration / all pairs
lessons.change: Print each unordered pair once (i < j only).
lessons.stretch: How many pairs if the array has 4 values, using i != j?

lessons.title: Bubble sort
lessons.idea: Each pass swaps neighbours that are out of order. Large values move right.
lessons.cue: Copy the array after every swap. Then after each pass.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
a <- [4, 1, 3, 2]
n <- 4
FOR pass <- 1 TO n - 1
    FOR i <- 0 TO n - 1 - pass
        IF a[i] > a[i + 1] THEN
            temp <- a[i]
            a[i] <- a[i + 1]
            a[i + 1] <- temp
        ENDIF
    NEXT i
NEXT pass
OUTPUT a
predict: What is a at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It repeatedly swaps adjacent items until the array is in order.
lessons.name: bubble sort
lessons.change: Sort descending instead. Flip the comparison.
lessons.stretch: How many neighbour comparisons happen for n = 4 with this code?
lessons.key: After pass 1: [1, 3, 2, 4]. Final: [1, 2, 3, 4]. Comparisons: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

lessons.title: Selection sort
lessons.idea: Each pass finds the smallest remaining value and swaps it into place.
lessons.cue: Mark the unsorted start. Track minPos through the inner loop.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
a <- [4, 1, 3, 2]
n <- 4
FOR i <- 0 TO n - 2
    minPos <- i
    FOR j <- i + 1 TO n - 1
        IF a[j] < a[minPos] THEN
            minPos <- j
        ENDIF
    NEXT j
    temp <- a[i]
    a[i] <- a[minPos]
    a[minPos] <- temp
NEXT i
OUTPUT a
predict: What is minPos when i is 0?
What is a after the first swap?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It selects the smallest leftover value and puts it at the next front slot.
lessons.name: selection sort
lessons.change: Select the largest remaining value and fill from the right.
lessons.stretch: Does it still swap when the smallest is already at i?
lessons.key: When i is 0, minPos becomes 1. After first swap: [1, 4, 3, 2]. Final: [1, 2, 3, 4]. Yes, it still swaps a slot with itself.

lessons.title: Complexity intuition
lessons.idea: Linear search grows with n. Binary search grows much slower on a sorted list.
lessons.cue: Do not start with Big O. Ask how much work for 10, then 100.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
FUNCTION linearSearch(arr, target)
    FOR i <- 0 TO LEN(arr) - 1
        IF arr[i] = target THEN
            RETURN i
        ENDIF
    NEXT i
    RETURN -1
ENDFUNCTION
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

snippets.label: Binary search shape
snippets.code:
FUNCTION binarySearch(arr, target)
    low <- 0
    high <- LEN(arr) - 1
    WHILE low <= high
        mid <- (low + high) DIV 2
        IF arr[mid] = target THEN
            RETURN mid
        ENDIF
        IF arr[mid] < target THEN
            low <- mid + 1
        ELSE
            high <- mid - 1
        ENDIF
    ENDWHILE
    RETURN -1
ENDFUNCTION
predict: About how many mid checks for 100 sorted values?
What if the array is not sorted?
snippets.printNote: Compare work with the linear version. Do not name Big O yet.

lessons.explain: Linear search may look at every item. Binary search halves the remaining items.
lessons.name: linear vs binary / work size
lessons.change: What if the target is first? What if it is absent?
lessons.stretch: Why does binary search need sorted data?
lessons.key: Linear worst: 10, then 100. Binary worst is about 4, then 7. Absent is worst for both. First item is best for linear, not special for binary.

lessons.title: Stack: push and pop
lessons.idea: A stack is last-in, first-out. Push adds on top. Pop removes the top.
lessons.cue: Draw the stack as a column. The top is the last item.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
stack <- []
PUSH stack, "A"
PUSH stack, "B"
PUSH stack, "C"
OUTPUT POP stack
OUTPUT POP stack
OUTPUT stack
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: The last item pushed is the first item popped.
lessons.name: stack / LIFO
lessons.change: Push D after the first pop. What is the next pop?
lessons.stretch: What happens if you pop an empty stack?
lessons.key: Prints C, then B. stack ends as [A].

lessons.title: Stack: reverse a word
lessons.idea: Push every letter, then pop them all. The letters come out backwards.
lessons.cue: Show the stack after the whole word is pushed, then after each pop.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
stack <- []
word <- "cat"
FOR i <- 0 TO LEN(word) - 1
    PUSH stack, word[i]
NEXT i
out <- ""
WHILE NOT ISEMPTY(stack)
    out <- out + POP stack
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT out
predict: What is on the stack after the FOR loop?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It stores the letters, then rebuilds the word from the top of the stack.
lessons.name: stack reverse
lessons.change: Reverse "stack" with the same method.
lessons.stretch: What is out for a one-letter word?
lessons.key: After the FOR: [c, a, t] with t on top. out is tac.

lessons.title: Stack: matching brackets
lessons.idea: Push an opener. Pop when you see a closer. A leftover or a short stack is a fail.
lessons.cue: Trace one character at a time. Stop talking in whole-string guesses.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
stack <- []
text <- "(())"
ok <- TRUE
FOR i <- 0 TO LEN(text) - 1
    IF text[i] = "(" THEN
        PUSH stack, "("
    ELSE
        IF ISEMPTY(stack) THEN
            ok <- FALSE
        ELSE
            POP stack
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
NEXT i
IF NOT ISEMPTY(stack) THEN
    ok <- FALSE
ENDIF
OUTPUT ok
predict: Is the stack empty at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: Each closer must match a previous opener that is still open.
lessons.name: stack matching
lessons.change: Trace ")(" and "(()". Why do both fail?
lessons.stretch: Extend the idea to () and [] together. What extra do you store on the stack?
lessons.key: For (()) the stack ends empty. ok is TRUE. )( fails on the first closer. (() fails because one opener remains.

lessons.title: Queue
lessons.idea: A queue is first-in, first-out. Enqueue joins the back. Dequeue leaves the front.
lessons.cue: Draw a line of people. The first arrival is served first.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
queue <- []
ENQUEUE queue, "Ali"
ENQUEUE queue, "Bea"
ENQUEUE queue, "Cal"
OUTPUT DEQUEUE queue
OUTPUT queue
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: The first person in the line is the first person out.
lessons.name: queue / FIFO
lessons.change: Dequeue twice. Who is left?
lessons.stretch: How is this different from the stack in Day 25?
lessons.key: Ali leaves first. queue ends as [Bea, Cal].

lessons.title: Queue processing
lessons.idea: Process jobs in arrival order until the queue is empty.
lessons.cue: Output each job as it is dequeued. Do not reorder.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
jobs <- []
ENQUEUE jobs, "print"
ENQUEUE jobs, "scan"
ENQUEUE jobs, "email"
WHILE NOT ISEMPTY(jobs)
    job <- DEQUEUE jobs
    OUTPUT job
ENDWHILE
predict: What is jobs at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It serves each waiting job in first-in, first-out order.
lessons.name: queue processing
lessons.change: A new job "copy" arrives after print is done. Where does it sit?
lessons.stretch: What if you used a stack for jobs instead?
lessons.key: Prints print, scan, email. jobs ends empty. A late copy job sits at the back.

lessons.title: Linked list: pointers
lessons.idea: A node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. NULL means stop.
lessons.cue: Draw boxes and arrows. Follow next with a finger.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nodeA.value <- "A"
nodeA.next <- nodeB
nodeB.value <- "B"
nodeB.next <- nodeC
nodeC.value <- "C"
nodeC.next <- NULL
OUTPUT nodeA.next.value
OUTPUT nodeA.next.next.value
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: You reach later nodes by following next, not by an index.
lessons.name: node / pointer / NULL
lessons.change: What is nodeC.next? What is nodeB.next.value?
lessons.stretch: If nodeA.next is set to nodeC, what happens to nodeB?
lessons.key: Prints B, then C. nodeC.next is NULL. Redirecting A to C skips B unless something else points at B.

lessons.title: Linked-list traversal
lessons.idea: Start at the head. Print the value. Move to next. Stop at NULL.
lessons.cue: current is the only moving part. Write it after every move.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
current <- nodeA
WHILE current != NULL
    OUTPUT current.value
    current <- current.next
ENDWHILE
predict: What is current at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It visits every node until there is no next node.
lessons.name: linked-list traversal
lessons.change: Print the list in reverse. What extra structure helps?
lessons.stretch: What happens if you write WHILE current.next != NULL by mistake?
lessons.key: Prints A, B, C. current ends as NULL. A next-only test would skip the last node.

lessons.title: Linked-list search
lessons.idea: Walk the nodes. Stop when the value matches, or when you hit NULL.
lessons.cue: Same shape as linear search, but move with next.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
current <- nodeA
target <- "B"
found <- FALSE
WHILE current != NULL AND found = FALSE
    IF current.value = target THEN
        found <- TRUE
    ELSE
        current <- current.next
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT found
predict: Where is current when it stops?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It scans nodes in order until the target appears.
lessons.name: linked-list search
lessons.change: Search for "D". What are found and current?
lessons.stretch: Why must you move current only in the ELSE?
lessons.key: found is TRUE. current is nodeB. For D, found is FALSE and current is NULL. Moving after a match would lose the node you found.

lessons.title: Linked-list insertion
lessons.idea: To insert after a node, point the new node at the old next, then swing the old next pointer.
lessons.cue: Draw before and after. Order of the two pointer writes matters.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
newNode.value <- "X"
newNode.next <- nodeA.next
nodeA.next <- newNode
predict: What does A point to after this?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It links X between A and the node that used to follow A.
lessons.name: linked-list insert
lessons.change: What goes wrong if you set nodeA.next <- newNode first?
lessons.stretch: Insert X at the front of the list. Which pointer is the head?
lessons.key: A points to X. X points to B. List is A -> X -> B -> C. If you swing A first, you lose B unless you saved it.

lessons.title: Hash map / dictionary
lessons.idea: A map stores key to value. You look up by key, not by position.
lessons.cue: Say the key, then the value. Avoid talking about index 0.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
scores <- {}
scores["Sam"] <- 12
scores["Jo"] <- 18
OUTPUT scores["Jo"]
scores["Sam"] <- 15
OUTPUT scores["Sam"]
predict: What is Sam's score at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It stores two named scores, then updates one of them.
lessons.name: dictionary / key-value
lessons.change: Add Lee with score 9. Output Lee.
lessons.stretch: What happens if you output scores["Pat"] when Pat was never stored?
lessons.key: Prints 18, then 15. Sam was overwritten, not added twice.

lessons.title: Frequency map
lessons.idea: A map can count. Each new key starts at 1. A seen key goes up by 1.
lessons.cue: After each word, write the whole map.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
words <- ["cat", "dog", "cat", "bird", "dog", "cat"]
freq <- {}
FOR EACH w IN words
    IF w IN freq THEN
        freq[w] <- freq[w] + 1
    ELSE
        freq[w] <- 1
    ENDIF
NEXT
OUTPUT freq
predict: What is freq after two words?
What is freq at the end?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It counts how often each word occurs.
lessons.name: frequency map / histogram
lessons.change: Count letters in "ababa" with the same idea.
lessons.stretch: Which key is the mode here?
lessons.key: After cat, dog: {cat:1, dog:1}. Final: cat 3, dog 2, bird 1. Mode is cat.

lessons.title: Recursive countdown
lessons.idea: A recursive call repeats the same work on a smaller input until a base case.
lessons.cue: Write one row per call. The base case is n = 0.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
PROCEDURE countdown(n)
    IF n = 0 THEN
        OUTPUT "done"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT n
        countdown(n - 1)
    ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

countdown(3)
predict: How many calls happen, including the first?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It prints n, then does the same job for n-1, until n is 0.
lessons.name: recursion / base case
lessons.change: Print n after the recursive call. What order do you get?
lessons.stretch: What happens if the base case is missing?
lessons.key: Prints 3, 2, 1, done. Calls: countdown(3), (2), (1), (0). Four calls.

lessons.title: Factorial
lessons.idea: The recursive case waits for a smaller answer, then multiplies.
lessons.cue: Fill the waiting-for column, then unwind the returns.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
FUNCTION factorial(n)
    IF n = 0 THEN
        RETURN 1
    ELSE
        RETURN n * factorial(n - 1)
    ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT factorial(4)
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: n! is n times the factorial of n-1. 0! is 1.
lessons.name: factorial / recursive case
lessons.change: Trace factorial(1) and factorial(2).
lessons.stretch: Why is the base 1, not 0?
lessons.key: factorial(0) returns 1. factorial(4) returns 24. Unwind: 1, 1, 2, 6, 24.

lessons.title: Fibonacci
lessons.idea: Two recursive calls can repeat the same work. Small n already shows the bush.
lessons.cue: Draw the call tree for fib(5). Circle repeated calls.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
FUNCTION fib(n)
    IF n <= 1 THEN
        RETURN n
    ELSE
        RETURN fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT fib(5)
predict: Which values are computed more than once?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: Each number is the sum of the two before it. The naive tree repeats fib(3) and fib(2).
lessons.name: fibonacci / repeated calls
lessons.change: How many times is fib(1) called for fib(5)?
lessons.stretch: How could a map store answers you already know?
lessons.key: fib(5) is 5. fib(3) and fib(2) repeat. fib(1) is called several times. A map is memoisation, name it after they see the repeats.

lessons.title: Recursive binary search
lessons.idea: The same half-and-check idea can be a function that calls itself on a smaller range.
lessons.cue: Link this to Day 20. low and high are now parameters.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
FUNCTION binSearch(arr, target, low, high)
    IF low > high THEN
        RETURN -1
    ENDIF
    mid <- (low + high) DIV 2
    IF arr[mid] = target THEN
        RETURN mid
    ENDIF
    IF arr[mid] < target THEN
        RETURN binSearch(arr, target, mid + 1, high)
    ELSE
        RETURN binSearch(arr, target, low, mid - 1)
    ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

OUTPUT binSearch([3, 8, 12, 19, 24], 19, 0, 4)
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It checks the middle, then recurses into the half that can still hold the target.
lessons.name: recursive binary search
lessons.change: Search for 3. Search for 11.
lessons.stretch: What is the base case for "not found"?
lessons.key: mid is 2 (value 12), then 3 (value 19). Returns 3. Not found when low > high.

lessons.title: Tree vocabulary
lessons.idea: A tree has one root. Nodes have children. A leaf has no children.
lessons.cue: Point at root, parent, child, leaf, and depth before any code run.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
nodeA.value <- "A"
nodeA.left <- nodeB
nodeA.right <- nodeC
nodeB.left <- nodeD
nodeB.right <- nodeE
nodeC.left <- NULL
nodeC.right <- NULL
nodeD.left <- NULL
nodeD.right <- NULL
nodeE.left <- NULL
nodeE.right <- NULL
predict: Who is the parent of E?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: A is the root. B and C are children of A. D and E hang from B. Leaves have no children.
lessons.name: root / child / parent / leaf / depth
lessons.change: What is the depth of D if the root is depth 0?
lessons.stretch: Is C a leaf here? Yes, both of its child pointers are NULL.
lessons.key: Root is A. Leaves are D, E, C. Parent of E is B. Depth of D is 2.

lessons.title: Binary trees
lessons.idea: A binary tree node has at most two children: left and right. A path is a walk down those links.
lessons.cue: Follow the code, not the picture in your head.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
current <- nodeA
OUTPUT current.value
current <- current.left
OUTPUT current.value
current <- current.right
OUTPUT current.value
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It starts at the root, steps left, then steps right from there.
lessons.name: binary tree / path
lessons.change: Write the steps that print A then C.
lessons.stretch: What happens if you step left from C?
lessons.key: Prints A, B, E. Path A -> B -> E. Left from C is NULL.

lessons.title: Binary search tree search
lessons.idea: In a BST, left is smaller, right is larger. Compare and walk one side.
lessons.cue: Use this tree: 10, left 6, right 15; 15 has left 12 and right 20.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
current <- root
target <- 12
WHILE current != NULL AND current.value != target
    IF target < current.value THEN
        current <- current.left
    ELSE
        current <- current.right
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
IF current = NULL THEN
    OUTPUT "absent"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "found"
ENDIF
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It walks toward the target by choosing the left or right child.
lessons.name: BST search
lessons.change: Search for 6. Search for 11.
lessons.stretch: Why does this fail if 15 sat on the left of 10?
lessons.key: Compares 10, then 15, then 12. Prints found. 11 walks 10 -> 15 -> 12 then left to NULL: absent.

lessons.title: Binary search tree insertion
lessons.idea: To insert, search until a NULL child. Hang the new node there.
lessons.cue: Same tree as Day 42. Insert 13. Ask which pointer changes.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
FUNCTION insert(node, value)
    IF node = NULL THEN
        newNode.value <- value
        newNode.left <- NULL
        newNode.right <- NULL
        RETURN newNode
    ENDIF
    IF value < node.value THEN
        node.left <- insert(node.left, value)
    ELSE
        node.right <- insert(node.right, value)
    ENDIF
    RETURN node
ENDFUNCTION

insert(root, 13)
predict: Which existing node gains a child?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: 13 is greater than 10 and less than 15 and greater than 12, so it becomes the right child of 12.
lessons.name: BST insert
lessons.change: Insert 7. Insert 15 again. What do you decide about duplicates?
lessons.stretch: Which pointer is the only one that changes for 13?
lessons.key: 12.right becomes 13. For 7: 6.right. Duplicates follow the ELSE here and go right.

lessons.title: Tree traversal
lessons.idea: In-order walks left, then the node, then right. On a BST that prints sorted values.
lessons.cue: Use the Day 42 tree. Write the call stack, not only the output.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
PROCEDURE inOrder(node)
    IF node != NULL THEN
        inOrder(node.left)
        OUTPUT node.value
        inOrder(node.right)
    ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

inOrder(root)
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It fully finishes the left subtree, prints the node, then does the right subtree.
lessons.name: in-order traversal
lessons.change: What would pre-order print (node, left, right) on the same tree?
lessons.stretch: Where does 20 appear, and why last?
lessons.key: Prints 6, 10, 12, 15, 20. 10 waits until its left child 6 is done. 20 is the last right-most node. Pre-order: 10, 6, 15, 12, 20.

lessons.title: Graph representation
lessons.idea: A graph is nodes plus connections. An adjacency list stores neighbours for each node.
lessons.cue: Read it as "who does this person know?" Do not assume a root.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
friends["Ali"] <- ["Bea", "Cal"]
friends["Bea"] <- ["Ali", "Dee"]
friends["Cal"] <- ["Ali"]
friends["Dee"] <- ["Bea"]
OUTPUT friends["Bea"]
predict: Is this graph directed or undirected as stored?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: Each person maps to a list of neighbours.
lessons.name: graph / adjacency list
lessons.change: Add a link between Cal and Dee. Which lists change if the graph is undirected?
lessons.stretch: Can a graph have a cycle? Point to one here.
lessons.key: Bea knows Ali and Dee. Stored both ways, so treat it as undirected. Cycle: Ali-Bea-Ali. Undirected add: Cal and Dee lists both gain a name.

lessons.title: Breadth-first search
lessons.idea: BFS uses a queue. It visits neighbours before it walks further out.
lessons.cue: Use the Day 45 graph. Start at Ali. Enqueue neighbours in list order.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
queue <- []
visited <- []
ENQUEUE queue, "Ali"
APPEND visited, "Ali"
WHILE NOT ISEMPTY(queue)
    person <- DEQUEUE queue
    OUTPUT person
    FOR EACH f IN friends[person]
        IF f NOT IN visited THEN
            ENQUEUE queue, f
            APPEND visited, f
        ENDIF
    NEXT
ENDWHILE
predict: Why does Cal appear before Dee?
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It explores the graph in layers: first Ali, then Ali's friends, then their new friends.
lessons.name: BFS / queue
lessons.change: Start at Dee instead. What order do you get?
lessons.stretch: Connect this to Day 28. Why a queue, not a stack?
lessons.key: Prints Ali, Bea, Cal, Dee. Cal is a neighbour of Ali, so Cal is in the first layer. Dee is one step further. Queue keeps that layer order.

lessons.title: Depth-first search
lessons.idea: DFS uses a stack. It walks one branch as deep as it can, then backtracks.
lessons.cue: Push neighbours in list order. The last pushed neighbour is popped first.

snippets.label: Main snippet
snippets.code:
stack <- []
visited <- []
PUSH stack, "Ali"
WHILE NOT ISEMPTY(stack)
    person <- POP stack
    IF person NOT IN visited THEN
        APPEND visited, person
        OUTPUT person
        FOR EACH f IN friends[person]
            PUSH stack, f
        NEXT
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
snippets.printNote: Predict first. Then trace every state change.

lessons.explain: It follows one neighbour chain first, because a stack returns the newest node.
lessons.name: DFS / stack
lessons.change: Start at Bea. Trace the stack.
lessons.stretch: Say the pairing: queue with BFS, stack with DFS.
lessons.key: Prints Ali, Cal, Bea, Dee. Ali pushes Bea then Cal, so Cal is popped first. Queue is BFS. Stack is DFS.
